results.corrected_title: Moonshot launches Kimi K3.1 Pro, near Claude Opus 5.5 on a coding benchmark, with open weights promised by 4 November
results.corrected_summary: On 23 October, China's Moonshot AI launched Kimi K3.1 Pro, a post-trained upgrade of its roughly 3-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model, plus a Highspeed variant it says runs two to three times faster. By Moonshot's own figures, which have not been independently verified, it scores 65.7 percent on Terminal-Bench 4.0, against 66.4 percent for Claude Opus 5.5 and 58.2 percent for GPT-6 Astra. Moonshot also says it beats both on the OfficeQA Pro v2 financial-analysis benchmark. Moonshot says it removed cyberattack-related training data before the open release, and it plans to publish the full weights by 4 November 2026.
key_facts: Launched 23 October 2026 in Kimi apps, the API and paid cloud services
Post-trained version of Kimi K3 (about 3 trillion parameters, released July 2026); Highspeed variant said to be 2-3x faster
Terminal-Bench 4.0 (Moonshot figures): K3.1 Pro 65.7%, Claude Opus 5.5 66.4%, GPT-6 Astra 58.2%
Moonshot says it beats both rivals on OfficeQA Pro v2 (no score published); it trails them on cybersecurity benchmarks
Open weights promised by 4 November 2026; cyberattack-related data removed from training
results.issues: Neither source confirms the 1-million-token context window, so it was removed. The 3 trillion parameters is K3's size; neither source states K3.1 Pro's own count. All benchmark numbers come from Moonshot and have not been independently verified. SiliconANGLE's headline misspells the name as 'Kim K3.1 Pro'.

results.corrected_title: Radical Numerics says AI-designed phages have been given to a patient for the first time
results.corrected_summary: On 20 October, San Francisco AI lab Radical Numerics announced Omnii-1, a multimodal genome language model. It says a phage cocktail designed with the model was given to one patient with an antibiotic-resistant bacterial infection, under an authorized, physician-led compassionate-use pathway. In lab tests the cocktail eliminated the patient's resistant bacterial isolate. The company has not disclosed the patient's outcome, citing privacy, and says one case cannot establish safety or efficacy.
key_facts: Announced 20 October 2026 on the Radical Numerics blog; model is called Omnii-1
Billed by the company as the world's first clinical use of AI-generated phages, under physician-led compassionate use
In vitro, the cocktail eliminated the patient's antibiotic-resistant isolate
Recovery (a proxy for viability) was 69.9% for designs with 11-15 amino acid changes, versus 4.8% for random controls
Patient outcome not disclosed; the therapy is not approved by regulators for broader use
results.issues: The 69.9% vs 4.8% figure applies only to designs with 11-15 amino acid changes, and it measures recovery (a proxy), not proven viability. The 'first' claim comes from the company and has not been independently confirmed. The Register notes the company did not answer its questions. Neither source names the physicians or institution.

results.corrected_title: Anthropic and Theorem: Claude formally proved 239 entry points in 123 open-source libraries crash-free and found hundreds of bugs
results.corrected_summary: On 22 October, Anthropic, working with verification company Theorem, said Claude wrote formal proofs that 239 fuzz-test entry points in 123 libraries from Google's OSS-Fuzz project cannot crash on any input under 64 MB. The proofs total about 180 million lines of Rocq and are checked against compiled RISC-V machine code. Writing them uncovered hundreds of bugs, including a logic bug that had gone unnoticed for more than a decade. Anthropic stresses that 'formally verified' does not mean bug-free, because the proofs rest on narrow assumptions.
key_facts: Published 22 October 2026 by Anthropic with Theorem
239 entry points across 123 OSS-Fuzz libraries proven crash-free for all inputs under 64 MB
About 180 million lines of Rocq proofs, checked against RISC-V executables
Hundreds of bugs found, including out-of-bounds writes and reads and a logic bug unnoticed for more than a decade
Assumptions: single-threaded static binaries, RISC-V, Linux with musl libc; individual proofs used hundreds of millions of tokens
results.issues: The specific claim that some bugs survived 'years of fuzzing' was not confirmed as worded. The sources support only a logic bug unnoticed for more than a decade, so the wording was softened. The Decoder's publication date is 2026-10-23.
